transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hello, doctor. My mind keeps getting stuck on "what if I missed something important and it harms me or my family," and I can’t seem to turn those thoughts off. It has become so exhausting to live with this constant worry.
Do you feel the need to perform certain actions or mental rituals to reduce the anxiety from these thoughts, like checking, counting, or repeating things?

Yes, I feel compelled to check things repeatedly just to ease that terrible anxiety. I find myself checking my pill organizer, medication list, calendar, and appointment cards four or five times before I can leave the house or go to bed. I just have to be absolutely sure I haven't made a mistake, but it really keeps me stuck.
Do these checking rituals take up a significant amount of your time each day—more than an hour—or cause distress that affects your daily life?

Yes, they take up a massive amount of time and cause so much distress, especially when checking my pill organizer and calendar keeps me up late at night. It slows me down so much that I've missed doctor's appointments and community events, and some days I just give up on going out altogether.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [F42, F41.1, F34.1], but based on this conversation, F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) and F34.1 (Dysthymia) are less likely because the patient's symptoms are dominated by intrusive, obsessive thoughts and repetitive, ritualistic behaviors aimed at reducing anxiety, which are hallmark features of F42 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder). The time consumption, distress, and functional impairment further support F42 as the primary diagnosis. No features suggestive of panic attacks, pervasive low mood, or chronic mild depression were endorsed to support the other candidates.
